CHAPTER XVIII. JOURNEY'S END



Darkness was beginning to gather slowly and with almost an apologetic
air, as if it regretted the painful duty of putting an end to the
perfect summer day. Over to the west beyond the trees there still
lingered a faint afterglow, and a new moon shone like a silver sickle
above the big barn. Sally came out of the house and bowed gravely three
times for luck. She stood on the gravel, outside the porch, drinking in
the sweet evening scents, and found life good.

The darkness, having shown a certain reluctance at the start, was now
buckling down to make a quick and thorough job of it. The sky turned
to a uniform dark blue, picked out with quiet stars. The cement of the
state road which led to Patchogue, Babylon, and other important centres
ceased to be a pale blur and became invisible. Lights appeared in the
windows of the houses across the meadows. From the direction of the
kennels there came a single sleepy bark, and the small white woolly dog
which had scampered out at Sally's heels stopped short and uttered a
challenging squeak.

The evening was so still that Ginger's footsteps, as he pounded along
the road on his way back from the village, whither he had gone to buy
provisions, evening papers, and wool for the sweater which Sally was
knitting, were audible long before he turned in at the gate. Sally could
not see him, but she looked in the direction of the sound and once again
felt that pleasant, cosy thrill of happiness which had come to her every
evening for the last year.

“Ginger,” she called.

“What ho!”

The woolly dog, with another important squeak, scuttled down the drive
to look into the matter, and was coldly greeted. Ginger, for all his
love of dogs, had never been able to bring himself to regard Toto with
affection. He had protested when Sally, a month before, finding Mrs.
Meecher distraught on account of a dreadful lethargy which had seized
her pet, had begged him to offer hospitality and country air to the
invalid.

“It's wonderful what you've done for Toto, angel,” said Sally, as he
came up frigidly eluding that curious animal's leaps of welcome. “He's a
different dog.”

“Bit of luck for him,” said Ginger.

“In all the years I was at Mrs. Meecher's I never knew him move at
anything more rapid than a stately walk. Now he runs about all the
time.”

“The blighter had been overeating from birth,” said Ginger. “That was
all that was wrong with him. A little judicious dieting put him right.
We'll be able,” said Ginger brightening, “to ship him back next week.”

“I shall quite miss him.”

“I nearly missed him--this morning--with a shoe,” said Ginger. “He was
up on the kitchen table wolfing the bacon, and I took steps.”

“My cave-man!” murmured Sally. “I always said you had a frightfully
brutal streak in you. Ginger, what an evening!”

“Good Lord!” said Ginger suddenly, as they walked into the light of the
open kitchen door.

“Now what?”

He stopped and eyed her intently.

“Do you know you're looking prettier than you were when I started down
to the village!”

Sally gave his arm a little hug.

“Beloved!” she said. “Did you get the chops?”

Ginger froze in his tracks, horrified.

“Oh, my aunt! I clean forgot them!”

“Oh, Ginger, you are an old chump. Well, you'll have to go in for a
little judicious dieting, like Toto.”

“I say, I'm most awfully sorry. I got the wool.”

“If you think I'm going to eat wool...”

“Isn't there anything in the house?”

“Vegetables and fruit.”

“Fine! But, of course, if you want chops...”

“Not at all. I'm spiritual. Besides, people say that vegetables are good
for the blood-pressure or something. Of course you forgot to get the
mail, too?”

“Absolutely not! I was on to it like a knife. Two letters from fellows
wanting Airedale puppies.”

“No! Ginger, we are getting on!”

“Pretty bloated,” agreed Ginger complacently. “Pretty bloated. We'll be
able to get that two-seater if things go buzzing on like this. There was
a letter for you. Here it is.”

“It's from Fillmore,” said Sally, examining the envelope as they went
into the kitchen. “And about time, too. I haven't had a word from him
for months.”

She sat down and opened the letter. Ginger, heaving himself on to the
table, wriggled into a position of comfort and started to read his
evening paper. But after he had skimmed over the sporting page he
lowered it and allowed his gaze to rest on Sally's bent head with a
feeling of utter contentment.

Although a married man of nearly a year's standing, Ginger was still
moving about a magic world in a state of dazed incredulity, unable fully
to realize that such bliss could be. Ginger in his time had seen many
things that looked good from a distance, but not one that had borne the
test of a closer acquaintance--except this business of marriage.

Marriage, with Sally for a partner, seemed to be one of the very few
things in the world in which there was no catch. His honest eyes glowed
as he watched her. Sally broke into a little splutter of laughter.

“Ginger, look at this!”

He reached down and took the slip of paper which she held out to him.
The following legend met his eye, printed in bold letters:

                                 POPP'S

                              OUTSTANDING

                 SUCCULENT----APPETIZING----NUTRITIOUS.



                        (JUST SAY “POP!” A CHILD

                              CAN DO IT.)



Ginger regarded this cipher with a puzzled frown.

“What is it?” he asked.

“It's Fillmore.”

“How do you mean?”

Sally gurgled.

“Fillmore and Gladys have started a little restaurant in Pittsburg.”

“A restaurant!” There was a shocked note in Ginger's voice. Although
he knew that the managerial career of that modern Napoleon, his
brother-in-law, had terminated in something of a smash, he had
never quite lost his reverence for one whom he considered a bit of a
master-mind. That Fillmore Nicholas, the Man of Destiny, should have
descended to conducting a restaurant--and a little restaurant at
that--struck him as almost indecent.

Sally, on the other hand--for sisters always seem to fail in proper
reverence for the greatness of their brothers--was delighted.

“It's the most splendid idea,” she said with enthusiasm. “It really does
look as if Fillmore was going to amount to something at last. Apparently
they started on quite a small scale, just making pork-pies...”

“Why Popp?” interrupted Ginger, ventilating a question which was
perplexing him deeply.

“Just a trade name, silly. Gladys is a wonderful cook, you know, and she
made the pies and Fillmore toddled round selling them. And they did
so well that now they've started a regular restaurant, and that's a
success, too. Listen to this.” Sally gurgled again and turned over the
letter. “Where is it? Oh yes! '... sound financial footing. In fact, our
success has been so instantaneous that I have decided to launch out on
a really big scale. It is Big Ideas that lead to Big Business. I am
contemplating a vast extension of this venture of ours, and in a very
short time I shall organize branches in New York, Chicago, Detroit, and
all the big cities, each in charge of a manager and each offering as
a special feature, in addition to the usual restaurant cuisine, these
Popp's Outstanding Pork-pies of ours. That done, and having established
all these branches as going concerns, I shall sail for England and
introduce Popp's Pork-pies there...' Isn't he a little wonder!”

“Dashed brainy chap. Always said so.”

“I must say I was rather uneasy when I read that. I've seen so many of
Fillmore's Big Ideas. That's always the way with him. He gets something
good and then goes and overdoes it and bursts. However, it's all right
now that he's got Gladys to look after him. She has added a postscript.
Just four words, but oh! how comforting to a sister's heart. 'Yes, I
don't think!' is what she says, and I don't know when I've read anything
more cheering. Thank heaven, she's got poor dear Fillmore well in hand.”

“Pork-pies!” said Ginger, musingly, as the pangs of a healthy
hunger began to assail his interior. “I wish he'd sent us one of the
outstanding little chaps. I could do with it.”

Sally got up and ruffled his red hair.

“Poor old Ginger! I knew you'd never be able to stick it. Come on, it's
a lovely night, let's walk to the village and revel at the inn. We're
going to be millionaires before we know where we are, so we can afford
it.”


THE END






End of Project Gutenberg's The Adventures of Sally, by P. G. Wodehouse

Darkness crept over the countryside with all the awkward politeness of a party guest who’s just realized he’s outstayed his welcome, almost apologetic for having to snuff out what had been a perfect, sun-warmed summer day. West of the treeline, a faint pink afterglow still lingered like a half-empty glass of lemonade, and the new moon glinted sharp as a silver sickle bobbing over the big red barn roof.

Sally stepped out onto the porch gravel and bowed three times very gravely for luck, then breathed in deep lungfuls of sweet clover and cut grass. Life, she decided, was pretty much unbeatable right now. The skittish darkness, having dragged its feet at the start, soon got down to business, painting the sky a rich dark blue dotted with soft, twinkling stars. The pale smear of the state road leading off to Patchogue and Babylon vanished into the dark, and little yellow windows began to glow in the farmhouses scattered across the meadows. A sleepy single bark drifted over from the kennels, and the tiny fluffy white dog that had scampered out at Sally’s heels puffed out its chest and let out a ferocious squeak that would have terrified a dandelion, if dandelions had a sense of self-preservation.

The evening was so dead still that Ginger’s heavy clomping footsteps could be heard trundling down the road long before he turned in at the gate. He’d headed to the village an hour before to pick up provisions, the evening papers, and the bright blue wool Sally was halfway through knitting him a sweater out of, and Sally didn’t even need to see him to get that soft, warm little happy thrill that had wrapped around her every single evening for the past year.

“Ginger!” she called.
“WHAT HO!” he yelled back.

The tiny white dog—Toto, formerly the most lethargic pet in three counties—scuttled down the drive to investigate, still squeaking like a squeaky toy with something to prove. Ginger, for all his deep and abiding love of all canines, had never once warmed to Toto, and dodged the little furball’s leaps of welcome like he was avoiding a cactus. He’d protested loudly when Sally, who’d found their neighbor Mrs. Meecher in tears a month prior over her pet’s mysterious refusal to move faster than a snail on Valium, had volunteered to give the little guy country air and a strict diet.

“You’ve worked absolute miracles on him, angel,” Sally laughed, as he came up the steps still side-stepping Toto’s attempts to lick his ankle. “He’s a whole new dog!”
“Lucky little blighter,” Ginger grumbled. “All the years I boarded at Mrs. Meecher’s he never moved faster than a stately grandad on a Sunday stroll. Now he’s bouncing off the walls 24/7.”
“Turns out the little gremlin had been overeating cake crumbs from birth,” Ginger said, brightening. “That’s all that was wrong with him. A bit of no-nonsense dieting fixed him right up. We can ship him back to Mrs. Meecher next week, thank the Lord.”
“I’m going to miss him,” Sally said.
“Nearly missed him with my work boot this morning,” Ginger said darkly. “Caught him up on the kitchen counter halfway through a full heist of our breakfast bacon. Took emergency measures.”
“My caveman,” Sally cooed, squeezing his arm. “I always said you had a horribly brutal streak. Ginger, isn’t this the most perfect evening ever?”

“Good Lord,” Ginger blurted out suddenly the second they stepped into the warm glow of the open kitchen door. He stopped dead and stared at her, wide-eyed. “You know you look even prettier than you did when I left for the village ten minutes ago?”

Sally gave his arm a squeeze. “Beloved! Did you remember the chops?”

Ginger froze. His face dropped like a rock off a pier. “Oh my aunt! I clean forgot the chops.”
“Oh Ginger, you absolute old chump. Well, looks like you’re signing up for the same judicious dieting program as Toto for dinner tonight.”
“I’m so sorry! I remembered the blue wool, though!”
“If you think I’m chewing on knitting supplies for dinner—”
“Wait, what’s even left in the house?”
“Root vegetables and a bowl of pears,” Sally said cheerfully.
“Fine by me! Though if you really wanted chops I could sprint back to the village—”
“Not at all, I’m very spiritual. Besides, everyone says vegetables are great for the blood pressure or something. Wait—you forgot the mail too, right?”
“Absolutely not! I was on that mail like a hungry seagull on a french fry. Two letters from people wanting to buy Airedale puppies off us.”
“No! Ginger, we’re actually making it!”
“Pretty much rolling in cash at this rate,” Ginger agreed, preening a little. “If we keep this up we can buy that shiny little two-seater car we’ve been gushing over for months. There’s a letter for you, too. Here.”

“It’s from Fillmore!” Sally said, turning the envelope over in her hands as they trundled into the kitchen. “About time, too. I haven’t heard a peep from him in months.”

She sat down and tore the envelope open. Ginger hauled himself up onto the kitchen table, wiggled into a comfortable spot, and flipped open his evening paper. He skimmed the sports page in two minutes flat, then let the paper lower to stare at Sally’s bent head, brimming over with that soft, dazed contentment he still couldn’t believe was real, even after nearly a year of marriage. He’d chased after dozens of fun-looking things in his life that had all turned out to be duds up close, but marrying Sally? That was the first thing that was even better than it looked. No catches, no fine print, no nasty surprises.

Sally suddenly snort-laughed. “Ginger, look at this!”

He leaned down and took the slip of paper she held out. Bold black letters glared up at him:

“What in the world is that?” he frowned.
“It’s Fillmore!” Sally cackled. “He and Gladys opened a little restaurant in Pittsburgh.”

“A restaurant?” Ginger’s voice was full of outright shock. He’d always thought Fillmore, Sally’s brother, was a bona fide mastermind even after his fancy corporate manager gig had crashed and burned, and the idea of the self-proclaimed “Man of Destiny” running a tiny restaurant struck him as almost indecent.

Sally, for her part, was absolutely delighted. “It’s the most brilliant idea he’s ever had! He’s finally doing something that makes sense! They started tiny, just selling homemade pork pies out of a cart—”
“Why Popp?” Ginger asked, the question eating at his brain.
“Trade name, silly. Gladys is an amazing cook, remember? She baked all the pies, Fillmore wandered around peddling them, and they blew up so fast they got a full restaurant now. And it’s doing gangbusters. Listen to this.” Sally flipped a page of the letter, snickering again. “‘We’re on a rock-solid financial footing. Our success was so instant that I’m planning to expand on a massive scale. Big Ideas make Big Business! I’m going to open branches in New York, Chicago, Detroit, every major city, each run by a manager, all serving our famous Popp’s Outstanding Pork-pies alongside regular menu items. Once that’s done, I’m sailing for England to take over the European pie market...’ Isn’t he just the cutest little go-getter?”
“Total genius. Always said so.”
“I was about to panic halfway through reading, honestly. I’ve seen so many of Fillmore’s Big Ideas go completely off the rails right when they’re doing well. But thank heaven Gladys has him well in hand. She added a postscript of exactly four words that’s the most comforting thing I’ve read all year. It says ‘Yes, I don’t think!’ So no cross-country pork pie empire any time soon, thank goodness.”

“Pork pies,” Ginger said dreamily, as very loud healthy hunger pangs started rumbling in his stomach. “Man, I wish he’d sent us one of those outstanding little chaps. I could devour the whole thing in two bites.”

Sally stood up and ruffled his bright red hair. “Poor old Ginger, I knew the vegetable plan wasn’t gonna fly. C’mon, it’s a perfect night. Let’s walk to the village inn and stuff ourselves silly. We’re gonna be puppy millionaires before we know it, we can absolutely afford the splurge.”
